To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of SNP array data to identify CNV in the human genome has led to the discovery of many CNVs that contribute to the etiology of common human diseases.
CNV are associated with common disease, and that GWAS are a powerful tool to discover such associations.

Genome-wide association studies (using single-nucleotide polymorphism arrays) are being extended to include copy-number variation (SNP arrays are designed to detect both single-nucleotide and copy-number variation).
In summary, our research is concerned with
extending genome-wide association studies from the realm of single nucleotide polymorphism to the realm of copy-number variation.
the identification of genetic factors that contribute to common diseases and the development of new methods to identify such genetic factors.
the identification and analysis of CNVs that contribute to disease susceptibility and with understanding the mechanisms by which CNVs affect disease susceptibility.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CNVs contribute to the genetic risk of common disease, and that the contribution is likely to be substantial.
the field is still in its infancy and that the future is bright.
GWAS have been extended to include CNV, and that this extension has already yielded important discoveries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human genome is not only made of SNPs but also of CNV, which can be used to study human diseases.
we have demonstrated the feasibility of GWAS for CNV.

the field has moved from a situation of being unable to detect CNVs in genome-wide association studies, through a period of intense methodological development and to a point where CNV analysis is a routine part of the analysis of GWAS data.
The main takeaway from our work is that

CNV is a major source of genetic variation that can contribute to common disease risk, and that GWAS can be used to discover the contribution of both de novo CNV and inherited CNV to risk of common disease.

it is possible to use the same GWAS data and analytical tools to discover CNV associations with disease, and that the same tools can be used to discover CNV in the general population that may contribute to disease risk.
the contribution of CNVs to disease risk is not trivial.
